newsitem.title: CHINA: China plans shot in arm for property sector - paper.
newsitem.headline: China plans shot in arm for property sector - paper.

text.p: China is expected to pass a series of measures by the end of this year aimed at bolstering its flagging property sector, the Business Weekly said on Sunday.
The measures would include boosting credit to property developers and reducing taxes on the sector, the newspaper quoted Pan Qiyuan, secretary-general of the China Real Estate Association, as saying.
The State Council, or cabinet, was now considering a number of new policies for the property industry and was likely to pass a series of measures by the end of the year, Pan said.
He said China would reduce levies on the sector and move to slash prices on unsold commercial housing to around cost.
"The anticipated government measures target affordable, commercially built housing," said the newspaper, which is published by the official China Daily.
Pan said the measures could make it easier for buyers to get mortgages. He gave no further details of the measures.
But in a related article, the newspaper quoted Lin Zengjie, executive director of the China Land Society, as saying China was still unsuited to mortgage loans.
"Conditions in China are not yet ripe (for mortgages) due to high interest rates and a lack of policies and supporting funds from the government," Lin said.
China's central bank recently ordered commercial banks to stop making consumer loans to finance property and car sales.

Lin said the State Planning Commission had also cut administrative fees for utilities, roads and telecommunications. This could make more money available to consumers to buy homes, the newspaper said without elaborating.
China spent about 200 billion yuan ($24.1 billion) a year on building residential housing, just one percent of annual consumer expenditure, the newspaper said.
Beijing would try to maintain growth of residential housing construction at 15 percent a year up to 2000, it added.
China aimed to build 3.0 billion square metres of new housing and renovate 2.9 billion square metres of old and dangerous housing by 2000, the paper said.
